children: Dutch buyout firm Main Capital Partners agreed to acquire TCV-backed educational technology platform Watermark Insights, clinching its largest U.S. bet to date on a company and a corner of the market it deems safe from AI disruption.
The deal is Main Capital's largest in the U.S. since it opened an office in the country in 2023.

A person familiar with the deal said the combined enterprise value for Watermark and UK-based educational support business Tribal Group-which Main Capital agreed to acquire last week for about $256 million-approached $600 million, including debt.
Main Capital is now acquiring "a substantial majority stake" in Watermark, which was formed in 2018 through the merger of several higher-education software companies, including Taskstream and Tk20.
Tech investor TCV acquired a controlling stake in Watermark that year.

Main Capital Partner Daan Visscher said the Watermark and Tribal Group acquisitions reflect the firm's view of the attractive dynamics it sees in the education market. Higher education institutions consistently face operational hurdles, from tight budgets to changing regulations and complex data requirements, said Visscher, who co-heads the firm's North America operations.
"There is a lot of need to further optimize their internal processes, and we also believe that AI can help with that," he said.

While artificial intelligence has chilled dealmaking across the broader software market, buyout shops like Main Capital bet edtech software supports mission-critical systems of record-managing accreditation, compliance, and core administrative work-and are largely insulated from AI displacement. Further, investors and consultants say edtech companies stand to benefit from workflow automation and new AI products and offer recurring revenue streams regardless of the economy's ups and downs.

The number of education deals in North America is growing again following the Covid pandemic-driven highs of 2021, according to advisory firm L.E.K. Consulting. L.E.K. tracked about $5.8 billion worth of education deals across some 72 transactions in 2025. But the firm noted the pipeline is shoring up, with the number of deals valued under $1 billion in 2025 reaching the highest level since 2021.
Based in Austin, Texas, Watermark has more than 300 employees and serves some 1,500 higher education institutions globally, including Princeton, Purdue, and Seton Hall universities.

Watermark's intelligence-powered software helps colleges and universities manage their administrative and academic operations. This includes automating some paperwork, helping schools develop and refine curricula, tracking student performance, and gathering the data schools need to obtain and maintain accreditation.
The company currently generates about $70 million to $100 million in annual recurring revenue, which is growing at a double-digit percentage, Visscher said.

A popular metric for software-as-a-service companies is the "Rule of 40," which holds that revenue growth and profit margin should add up to at least 40%. Watermark meets that rule, Main Capital Managing Partner Sjoerd Aarts said, adding that the private-equity firm doubled down on the software sector even as AI fears drove a market selloff at the beginning of the year.

At the time, the firm was fundraising and amassed EUR5.25 billion, or about $6 billion, across two funds, nearly doubling its assets under management. Aarts said the firm's long experience investing in technology and detailed knowledge of its portfolio company operations have given it confidence it can pick AI winners, such as Watermark and Tribal Group.
Main Capital sees ample room to grow Watermark, including by expanding the company's operations into Europe.

Arts, who heads the firm's Benelux and U.K. operations, said he expects to see a big increase in private market software investing driven by the recognition that many software companies stand to gain from the AI revolution.
"The dust around AI is settling," he said.
